highlights: Retro-glamorous Sardinian icon with whitewashed curves, emerald bays and dazzling beachside dining
description:
Romazzino sits above a pale, sheltered bay on Sardinia's Costa Smeralda, at Via Romazzino in Arzachena, close to Porto Cervo and the granite coves and translucent water that made this stretch of coast famous. The hotel is one of the area’s original icons, conceived in the 1960s as a whitewashed Mediterranean village where terraces, gardens and beach life blur into one another.

Its low, sculptural architecture keeps the profile close to the hillside, with rounded volumes, arched openings and sun-bleached interiors that echo Sardinian craft more than polished resort uniformity. Rooms, suites and villas are arranged with balconies or terraces towards sea or gardens; higher-category suites and villas add host service, secluded seafront positions or broad panoramic decks.

Dining leans into the island’s rhythm. La Terrasse brings refined Sardinian and Italian cooking to a bay-facing setting, Éntu e Mari works as a beach grill for long lunches by the water, and the Beach Bar, Ginepro Bar and Pool Bar stretch the day from espresso to evening aperitivi. Two outdoor pools, including a saltwater pool, frame the shoreline mood without competing with the beach.

The experience is deeply coastal but not static. The hotel can arrange boat trips through the La Maddalena archipelago, watersports, wine tastings, hikes on the Pevero Health Trail and excursions to Arzachena’s archaeological sites. A spa with sauna and steam room, yoga and Pilates studio, tennis and padel courts, and the relaxed glamour of Costa Smeralda’s boutiques round out a property that remains more cinematic than showy.

highlights: Pink clifftop grand dame with Atlantic gardens, sea pools and Michelin-starred Madeira dining
description:
Belmond Reid's Palace occupies a cliffside estate on Madeira’s Atlantic edge, just west of central Funchal and within easy reach of the city’s marina, market halls and subtropical gardens. Its salmon-pink façade has been part of island lore since the hotel first opened to guests in 1891, when Madeira sat on the grand-tour route between Europe, Africa and the Americas.

The 126 rooms and suites preserve a polished resort grandeur, balancing traditional detailing with balconies, terraces or garden-facing outlooks that make the ocean a constant presence. Mature palms, terraced lawns and flowering paths soften the scale of the building, while the setting keeps both Funchal’s historic centre and Madeira’s mountain trails close at hand.

Dining is unusually strong for a resort of this character. William Restaurant holds one Michelin star and gives the hotel a contemporary fine-dining anchor, while Ristorante Villa Cipriani looks to Italy from its sea-facing terrace. Brisa do Mar and the Pool Terrace keep the mood lighter, afternoon tea remains a signature ritual on the terrace, and the 1891 Bar and Tea Library move from Madeira classics to evening cocktails.

The leisure offer is rooted in the island’s climate. Three pools include seawater and heated options, with a tidal pool and sea platform connecting directly to the Atlantic. A spa, sauna, fitness centre, tennis courts and children’s club add depth, while guided botanical walks, golf outings, mountain hikes and excursions to Pico do Arieiro widen the sense of Madeira beyond the gardens. Few hotels on the island combine heritage, ocean access and gastronomy with such ease.

highlights: Colonial monastery sanctuary with candlelit cloisters, Andean art and Plazoleta Nazarenas drama
description:
Belmond Hotel Monasterio sits on Plazoleta Nazarenas in Cusco’s historic centre, five minutes on foot from the Plaza de Armas and close to the city’s cathedrals, museums and carved Inca walls. The address carries unusual gravity: a former monastery and seminary, protected as a national monument, at an altitude where the Andes feel present even inside the courtyards.

The 117 rooms and suites are arranged around cloisters, tiled roofs and a serene central courtyard shaded by an ancient cedar. Spanish-colonial architecture, stone arches and religious art set the tone, while alpaca textiles and oxygenated rooms in selected categories adapt the heritage setting to contemporary comfort. The San Antonio Abad chapel, still used for special events, adds to the building’s quiet ceremonial atmosphere.

Food keeps the hotel tied to Peru rather than to generic grand-hotel formality. OQRE, led by chef Jorge Muñoz, draws ingredients and ideas from the coast, highlands and jungle, while El Tupay serves refined international cooking beneath candlelit arches and is known for opera evenings. OQRE Bar turns towards pisco, Andean flavours and live jazz.

The hotel’s greatest facility is the sense of immersion in Cusco itself. Private art tours examine 17th-century Cusco School paintings and colonial religious works; cooking classes can begin at San Pedro Market before returning to the kitchen; and pisco lessons, Andean bath rituals and massages slow the pace after exploring the city. From here, the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are natural extensions, but the property never feels like a mere stopover. Its monastery walls hold a deeply local, contemplative version of Peruvian luxury.

highlights: Solar-powered tented lodge with waterhole hide, big-cat game drives and elephant-filled plains
description:
Belmond Savute Elephant Lodge lies deep in Botswana’s Chobe National Park, beside the unpredictable Savute Channel in a dry, elemental landscape of floodplains, sand ridges and open savanna. This is one of Chobe’s most dramatic wildlife corners, known for elephant herds, lion prides, wild dogs, leopards, cheetahs, hyenas and the seasonal movement of zebra across the plains.

The lodge is deliberately intimate, with 12 tented rooms raised on wooden platforms and oriented towards the channel and passing wildlife. Four-poster beds, private decks, shaded outdoor lounges and air conditioning soften the remoteness, while bamboo decking, solar power and handmade details bring a more considered sustainability language to the classic safari-camp silhouette. The atmosphere is elegant but exploratory rather than ornate.

Days revolve around the bush. Game drives track predators and elephant movements across Savute’s shifting terrain, while a dedicated lookout hide faces the waterhole for quieter watching between drives. Birding is excellent, with more than 250 recorded species, and excursions can add ancient San rock paintings, a grove of giant baobabs and sunset drinks among sand dunes.

Meals are served as part of the safari rhythm, from open-air breakfasts and generous lunches to African-accented dinners under wide skies. Evenings often gather around the campfire or at Mothupi’s Boma, where storytelling becomes part of the landscape. A spa tent, swimming pool and permanent-waterhole outlook add softness without diluting the wilderness. The result is a compact, highly focused lodge where the luxury is inseparable from access to one of southern Africa’s great wildlife stages.

highlights: Andes-framed urban resort with lush gardens, lagoon pool and polished Las Condes dining
description:
Mandarin Oriental Santiago is set on Presidente Kennedy Avenue in Las Condes, a polished business and residential district backed by the Andes. The address places it close to Parque Araucano, Parque Arauco’s luxury retail, corporate Santiago and the route east towards the ski valleys, while still feeling more like an urban resort than a conventional city hotel.

The building is one of Santiago’s modern landmarks and became Mandarin Oriental’s first property in South America. Its 299 spacious rooms and suites frame views of the city, gardens or mountains, with the best angles catching the Andes beyond the glass. Interiors are contemporary and calm, designed to temper the city’s energy with generous proportions, soft textures and a sense of indoor-outdoor space.

Dining is compact but international. Matsuri focuses on Nikkei cuisine, bringing Japanese technique into conversation with Peruvian and South American flavours; Senso serves Italian cooking with a strong wine identity; and the Atrium Lobby Lounge gives the hotel its social living room for light bites, cocktails and afternoon pauses. In-room dining completes the round-the-clock resort rhythm.

Wellness is central to the property’s identity. The grounds extend across 25,000 square metres, with landscaped gardens and a large lagoon-style outdoor pool that gives the hotel much of its leisure-resort character. A spa treatment programme, 24-hour fitness centre with Technogym equipment, outdoor spaces and proximity to Parque Araucano support a stay that can alternate between meetings, shopping and restorative downtime. For Santiago, the combination of scale, greenery and mountain-framed urban polish remains notably rare.
